title: How Strata-East worked: artists self-funded finished records
summary: Musicians brought finished products and invested in themselves, with no contracts, no art department and about 65 releases over roughly ten years.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Can I pause for a moment there. Are you saying that the artists had their recordings already completed and they came to you for whatever your label could offer?

Exactly. And see there was the misunderstanding, the rest of the industry had other musicians and everything during that time, up until today for a lot of them, because they never understood how it worked and the reason why is because I wanted it that way. I wanted it to have the look of a regular record company. And the assumption was that we were putting these artists under contract and issuing their product. I would never have had that kind of a venture. It was about the musician investing in himself. And becoming the major recipient of what came back. That’s how I function. So when this fellow who wrote this saying “on a minimal budget” it was less than a minimal budget. I mean if I think back I don’t know how I was able to negotiate the business in terms of having an office finally, to do all this. But I mean I was able to do that, I mean you know — if I was going to be a pharmacist, that meant that I was pretty good at chess, I was pretty good at chemistry and math. So you know you don’t have to only just be a musician. I think most musicians are pretty good at chess and those things too. It just so happened that I could multi-task at the drop of a hat so that’s the way it went. So yes, each musician, they would come and say, “Wow, I’d like to do that. How do you do that?” I said, “Well do you have a product all ready?” “Well not yet.” I’d say, “Go get one, go make one.” Or if they already knew that that was the deal they would come with it all ready, we’d listen to it and we’d say okay boom, you’re in, go.
Did you ever have someone come in with their product and say, “Well this has potential?” Did you get in a position where you started giving advice, try again, and make it more this or that?

No. So when they’d come it was wow man, okay, here’s a young fellow, he wants to do this, I’d listen to it and if it was decently recorded and the package was nice I might suggest you might want to do this with the cover or something. But all of them already saw the covers of things that had already come out so you know, there wasn’t an art department that created these things, they did.

That’s the beauty of it you know. And so the rest is history. And I mean at one point I think we had about 65 all told. And the deal was that if you’re unsatisfied, you know, with the result you know, you can take your product and start to do it yourself you know? Which did happen you know, with some of them. And that was fine. The whole idea was that it would be influential to enough musicians who were known and were working that the product would sell itself, because they’re working and avid to sell you know on their venues or whatever, besides the mom & pop distribution system you know that we had set up you know during those years. And this all went for about ten years you know. And around 1980 I decided to slow things down because I just needed to take a break. I had gone hard at that for ten years you know.
